1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: The natural main line: Black develops, guards d5 a second time and controls e4. Every set-up stays open, from taking the pawn on c4 to building the Semi-Slav chain, and White now decides whether the game is sharp or quiet.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 solidly but locks in the light-squared bishop, the piece the c6-pawn was meant to free. With the knight on f3 rather than c3, White can avoid the sharp lines Black hoped for and play a quiet, comfortable game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 a6.strategy: A flexible waiting move that prepares ...b5 and eases the development of the light-squared bishop. It commits to nothing in the centre, but it gives White time and the choice of set-up, including a fianchetto of the king's bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3.strategy: Meets the declined set-up solidly: the pawn opens the f1-bishop to defend c4, so ...dxc4 gains Black nothing. White keeps the b1-knight flexible and a small, safe edge, while Black's light-squared bishop stays shut in behind the pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2.strategy: Defends c4 with the queen instead of a pawn, so ...dxc4 loses its point while the c1-bishop is not yet boxed in by e3. The queen is somewhat exposed on c2, but White keeps a free choice between slow and sharp plans.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and heads for the full Semi-Slav set-up. White accepts that Black may now take on c4 and fight to keep the pawn, which leads to sharp, heavily analysed play with chances for both sides.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight, which guards d5 and controls e4, and keeps the Semi-Slav structure. Because White has not put a knight on c3, White still chooses the set-up from here.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nd7.strategy: Develops the queen's knight, which supports a later central break and leaves the king's knight free to choose its square. Black stays flexible, but White can also settle for a quiet set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once so that White must recapture with the bishop and Black can chase it with ...b5, gaining queenside space. The centre pawn is given up early and the c8 bishop stays behind e6, so Black must be ready for White's e4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nc3.strategy: The standard development, adding pressure on d5 and e4 and steering the game into the main line of the Semi-Slav, where the fight for the c4-pawn and the queenside decides. White commits the knight to c3 and accepts the sharp, strategically rich struggle.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Quiet Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.strategy: A quieter way to develop: the knight protects c4 and supports an e4 break while c3 stays free. White avoids the main-line theory for a slow, flexible game, and Black cannot count on the usual tempo-gaining capture on c4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.b3.strategy: Supports the c4-pawn with a pawn and prepares to bring the queen's bishop out on the long diagonal, free of the e3-pawn that hems it in now. It is a quiet, solid set-up that avoids the sharp main lines, but it asks little of Black.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.name: Semi-Slav Defence: Quiet Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.strategy: A flexible developing move that supports a later central break. Black waits for White to commit the bishop before taking on c4, so the gain of time when the bishop recaptures stays available.

Occupies e4 at once, though the knight is attacked by the d2-knight and defended only by the d-pawn, so Black must support it. The set-up gives Black a firm pawn chain and kingside space but a weak e5-square and a passive light-squared bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Spielmann Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.strategy: An unusual fianchetto that gives up the classical Semi-Slav set-up. It is solid but slow, and the bishop on g7 bites on a centre that White can still fill with pawns.
Develops the bishop to its best diagonal, aimed at h7, and prepares to castle. It also backs up a later e4 push by the knight, so White plays for a central expansion in a solid structure.

Backs up the c4-pawn from behind and looks down the diagonal to h7, while keeping the bishop's best square and the e4 push in reserve. White waits to see whether Black takes on c4, and the d2-knight can then recapture with a firm grip on the centre.

Guards the c4-pawn with a pawn and prepares to bring the queen's bishop out on the long diagonal, where the e3-pawn no longer blocks it. A sound but modest set-up: White commits the queenside pawns early and aims for a slow, solid game rather than a sharp fight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Semmering Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.strategy: Strikes at d4 before White has castled, trading the solid c6-support for activity. Black opens the centre and the d5-pawn may become isolated, so the move trades long-term solidity for freedom of play.

The thematic capture: Black gives up the centre pawn and drives the recapturing piece back with ...b5, winning time for queenside expansion. White gets the freer centre, Black the space and activity on the other wing, and a rich, double-edged middlegame follows.

Develops the bishop to a natural square pointing at h2 and supports a later ...e5, but it leaves the tension in the centre untouched. White can open the game with e4, and Black settles for a solid but rather passive position.
Attacks the e4-knight a second time: with the knight on d2, Nxe4 dxe4 Bxe4 would win a pawn. Black has to trade the knight or reinforce it at once.

Attacks the e4-knight a second time: the queen and the d2-knight both hit it, and only the d5-pawn guards it. Black must trade or reinforce at once, while White keeps the bishop free for its best square and a harmonious development.

A modest square for the bishop that prepares castling but adds nothing against the e4-knight, so Black can settle it with a trade or a pawn at leisure. White keeps a flexible, level position and cedes the initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Stonewall Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Nbd2.strategy: Reinforces the knight with a pawn chain on d5, e6 and f5. The knight has a stable outpost and Black gains kingside space, at the price of a weakened e5-square and a light-squared bishop that is hemmed in behind its own pawns.

Trades the advanced knight at once instead of defending it, which relieves Black's cramped position and keeps the pawn structure sound. Black gives up the outpost for peace of mind: a quiet game in which the c8-bishop still waits behind the pawns.

Retreats the knight instead of supporting it, which avoids weakening the e5-square. The knight covers c4 and f5, but White can chase it with c5, gaining space and time on the queenside, so Black has lost a tempo for a solid but passive set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, so White's queen has to recapture on c4, where pawn pushes and knight moves can chase it and gain time. Black gives up the tension in the centre in exchange for easy, tempo-gaining development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the capture on c4 in reserve for the moment it gains most. Black's centre stays solid and nothing is committed; the cost is that White chooses how to develop without being hurried by a pawn grab.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 Nd7.strategy: Develops the knight behind the centre and prepares ...e5. The c8-bishop is still shut in by the e6-pawn and now also by the d7-knight, so Black is solid but passive until ...b6 gives it the b7 square.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 dxc4 5.Qx.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with the queen and keeps the pawn centre intact. The price is a queen on c4 that Black can attack with tempo, so White has to develop with that in mind. The natural recapture, and the point of the queen move to c2.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 dxc4 5.e3.strategy: Plans to win the pawn back with the bishop while building the centre, but the recapture is not forced: Black can hold the extra pawn with ...b5, and White must then undermine it while dealing with ...Bb4+. A slower, less certain way to level the material than taking back at once.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 dxc4 5.e4.strategy: Goes for a broad centre and quick development instead of winning the pawn back at once. Black can hold the extra pawn with ...b5, so White must prove the initiative is worth it: a sharp, risky choice that leaves Black the easier game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Qc2 dxc4 5.Qx.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps ...b5 in reserve to gain time against the queen on c4, so White cannot develop freely. Black has a solid structure and easy play; the c8-bishop comes out later once the queenside pawns move.

Hits the queen at once and gains time for queenside expansion, since c6 guards the new pawn. It also frees b7 for the light-squared bishop that e6 had shut in. The cost is a looser queenside, because the b5-pawn depends on the c6-pawn alone.

Develops the knight and heads for a compact set-up, but it forgoes the chance to hit the queen at once. Black stays solid while White develops and then decides where the queen goes, so the move gives up the initiative Black could have claimed.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: The main line of the Slav: the knight adds pressure on d5 and makes an early ...Bf5 costly, because cxd5 followed by Qb3 attacks b7 and d5 together. White takes the most testing path, in which Black must decide how to meet the pressure on the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3.name: Slav Defence: Quiet Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3.strategy: A modest move: the pawn opens the light-squared bishop and defends c4 while the b1-knight stays flexible. It blocks in the c1-bishop, and White accepts a quieter game in which Black can bring the light-squared bishop out of the pawn chain.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nbd2.name: Slav Defence: Breyer Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Nbd2.strategy: A quiet developing move: the knight protects c4 and supports e4 while c3 stays free. White aims for a slow set-up with a kingside fianchetto instead of main-line theory, which gives Black time to bring the light-squared bishop out of the pawn chain.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2.strategy: Defends c4 with the queen and discourages ...Bf5, since the bishop would meet the queen on its diagonal. White keeps a flexible position, but the queen is somewhat exposed on c2.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3.strategy: Heads for a kingside fianchetto, but the move order is inaccurate: Black can develop the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain at once, so the fianchetto set-up is less effective than in lines where that bishop stays shut in.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5.strategy: Releases the tension at once and heads for a symmetrical pawn structure with an open c-file. White gives up the pressure on d5 and keeps only the extra move, so the game tends towards a quiet, drawish middlegame.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.name: Slav Defence: Bonet Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Bg5.strategy: A gambit that leaves c4 unprotected and the kingside undeveloped: Black can simply take the pawn, and the c6-pawn gives a base to hold it. White has to show compensation in development for the pawn.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5 cxd5.name: Slav Defence: Exchange Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5 cxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the c-pawn, restoring a symmetrical structure and opening the c-file. Black gives White only the first-move edge, and the middlegame tends to be quiet, with rooks and pieces traded down the file.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5 Nxd5.strategy: Recaptures with the knight, but e4 hits it with tempo and White gets a broad pawn centre while Black spends time moving the knight again. Black has given up the symmetrical structure for nothing in return.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where Nc3 attacks it with tempo. Black loses time with the queen while White develops, and nothing is gained for the lost moves.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.cxd5 cxd5 5..strategy: Develops and adds pressure on d5 while keeping the symmetrical structure intact. The extra move gives White only a small initiative, so this is a safe way to play for a slight pull rather than a win.

Develops the dark-squared bishop actively before the e-pawn can shut it in, taking aim at the dark squares and c7. The symmetrical structure stays and White hopes for the small edge of the extra move, though Black can develop calmly and keep the balance.

Attacks b7 and d5 together, but the c8-bishop guards b7 and the f6-knight guards d5, so nothing is won. The queen has no target, Black simply develops, and White has spent a move without improving the position.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5.name: Slav Defence: Quiet Variation, Schallopp Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5.strategy: Takes the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain, the Slav's idea, before ...e6 can lock it in. Black need not fear cxd5 and Qb3, because the f6-knight guards d5 and the queen's fork of b7 and d5 does not work.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bg4.name: Slav Defence: Quiet Variation, Pin Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the f3-knight against the queen. White has to deal with the pin soon, and Black is happy to trade the bishop for the knight if asked, in a solid but passive game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6.strategy: Heads for a Semi-Slav chain but shuts in the light-squared bishop. Since White has not put a knight on c3, White keeps useful alternatives and White's position is the more comfortable.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Nc3.strategy: The most testing development: the knight adds pressure on d5 and keeps the option of a sortie to chase the f5-bishop and win the bishop pair. White aims for a small, lasting edge while Black has a solid position.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.cxd.strategy: Releases the tension and heads for a symmetrical structure with the queen's sortie to b3 in reserve. White's dark-squared bishop stays boxed in by e3, and Black can meet the queen's raid comfortably.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Bd3.strategy: Offers to exchange the light-squared bishops, removing the piece Black has just brought out. The exchange gives White little to play for, so it is a safe route to a level, quiet game rather than a try for an edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.cxd.strategy: Recaptures with the c-pawn, keeping a symmetrical structure and the open c-file. The bishop on f5 is already developed, which makes this exchange safe for Black.

Recaptures with the knight, keeping the c-pawn, but b7 is loose now that the bishop has left c8. The queen sortie to b3 attacks it with nothing to guard it, so Black has to spend time on a defence and stays a step behind.
Recaptures with the queen, which White chases at once with Nc3. Black loses time and White develops with the initiative, with nothing gained in return.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.cxd.name: Slav Defence: Exchange Variation, Schallopp Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.cxd.strategy: Develops with pressure on d5 and keeps the queen's sortie in reserve. The structure is symmetrical, White's e3-pawn restricts the c1-bishop, and White plays for a small edge from the extra move.

Attacks b7 and d5 together, hoping to exploit that Black's bishop has left the queenside. The f6-knight guards d5, so Black only has to meet the threat to b7, and the sortie gives White no more than a small, active edge.
Offers to exchange the light-squared bishops, taking away Black's active piece. After the trade Black develops freely, and the symmetrical structure leaves White with no more than the extra move.
Shores up d5 and opens the f8-bishop, a solid way to meet the pressure. Black has a sturdy symmetrical-type structure and only has to watch for losing the bishop pair.

Develops the knight with pressure on d4 and keeps the symmetrical structure, but b7 is loose without the bishop on c8. Black must be ready for the queen sortie to b3, which hits b7 and puts d5 under strain.

Develops the second knight and covers b6 and e5, but it leaves b7 loose: the queen sortie to b3 hits it at once, with d5 also under fire from the queen and the c3-knight. Black can cope but is made to react.
Defends b7 from c8, but it is a passive square for the queen. It holds everything together, while White keeps the more active game.

Defends b7 along the rank and puts the queen on an active square, while the f6-knight guards d5, so the double attack is empty. Black keeps the symmetrical structure and completes development with an easy, level game.
Defends b7 by offering a queen trade. Taking on b6 leaves Black with doubled b-pawns in exchange for an open a-file, so Black gets a level endgame with a damaged pawn structure to look after.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Nc3.name: Slav Defence: Quiet Variation, Schallopp Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 Bf5 5.Nc3.strategy: Shores up d5 and opens the f8-bishop. White can win the bishop pair by chasing the f5-bishop with a knight, but Black gets a sound position with counterplay from a central break.
Takes b5 from the knight and prepares queenside expansion, but it neither supports d5 nor develops a piece. The queen sortie to b3 attacks b7 at once, and Black has to spend time answering it.
Releases the tension in the centre: White recaptures with the bishop on c4, a developing move, and Black must justify the exchange with queenside expansion while White enjoys the freer centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn while the fianchetto has not yet secured c4. White has to win it back with piece play, and Black has the c6-pawn as a base to hold it, but risks falling behind in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4.strategy: Gets the light-squared bishop out of the pawn chain at once and presses on the f3-knight that guards e5. Black accepts that White's fianchettoed bishop will fight for the long diagonal.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bf5.strategy: Brings the problem bishop outside the pawn chain, the point of the Slav, before White's move order can interfere. Black reaches a solid, level game in which the c8-bishop is no longer shut in, unlike in the closed set-ups White was aiming for.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 e6.strategy: Shuts the light-squared bishop in behind the pawn chain and invites a set-up where the fianchettoed bishop presses on d5 and the long diagonal. Solid, but it gives up the main point of ...c6, the free bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop supports the centre along the long diagonal and prepares castling. White accepts the pressure on the f3-knight in return for a harmonious set-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.cxd.strategy: Releases the tension and opens the c-file just when Black's bishop has left c8, so b7 has lost its guard. Whichever way Black recaptures, the queen sortie to b3 attacks b7, and Black has to react while White finishes development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.Ne5.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once, but it simply goes to f5, where it was heading anyway. The knight is well placed on e5 but can be challenged, and White has gained little for the time spent.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.Bg2.strategy: Finally supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop. The c8-bishop is already outside the pawn chain, so the move does not block it, and Black gets a solid structure.

Develops the second knight and covers e5, so the knight jump to e5 no longer gains time against the g4-bishop. Black keeps the pressure on the f3-knight and a flexible centre; the price is a slightly passive piece placement.

Takes the pawn, but White has a ready way to win it back: Ne5 hits the g4-bishop with gain of time. Black gives up the tension in the centre and spends a move on the capture without a clear follow-up.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.Bg2.name: Slav Defence: Modern Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 Bg4 5.Bg2.strategy: Tucks the king away and completes the kingside development. The bishop on g2 keeps the long diagonal pointed at Black's queenside, and White has a comfortable, harmonious game.

Brings the last knight into the game and adds pressure on d5 and e4, keeping the pawn centre in reserve for a later e4 or cxd5. White castles a move later, and Black's bishop on g4 has to decide whether to take the knight on f3.

Threatens the b7 pawn, which lost its guard when the bishop went to g4, and so forces Black to respond. Black can answer ...Qb6 and offer a queen exchange, and White has nothing clear to show for the early sortie, so the move is playable rather than best.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4 5.Bg.strategy: Develops the bishop to the long diagonal and prepares castling. White does not recapture at once: the c4-pawn is loose, Black must spend time to hold it, and White answers with pressure on the centre and queenside.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4 5.Na.strategy: Aims the knight at c4 to win the pawn back at once, before the fianchetto. Black can hold it with ...b5, but that loosens the queenside, and White undermines it with a4. The knight on the rim is the price of regaining the pawn quickly.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4 5.Qc.strategy: Eyes c4 with the queen and keeps the fianchetto in reserve. Black keeps the pawn with ...b5 and gains space on the queenside, while the queen on c2 has no other job and is exposed to a later ...Bf5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4 5.Bg.name: Slav Defence: Modern Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.g3 dxc4 5.Bg.strategy: Meets the fianchetto with a fianchetto of its own: the bishop on g7 contests the long diagonal and presses on d4. Black does not try to defend the c4-pawn directly and relies on development and counter-pressure.

The solid answer: it opens the way for the king's bishop, guards the centre and leaves Black two plans, holding the extra pawn with ...b5 or giving it back to free the position. White's bishop on g2 presses on the long diagonal, and Black has to meet that pressure with patient development.

Develops the last knight with the idea of ...Nb6, which defends the pawn on c4 without committing the pawns. Black keeps the structure compact and avoids the weaknesses that ...b5 brings, at the cost of a cramped position for the bishop on c8.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and keeps the tension in the centre. The bishop on c8 is shut in for the moment, but it can come out later via b7 once Black has taken on c4 and advanced the b-pawn. Black gains a solid centre at the cost of some freedom for that bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 dxc4.strategy: The main reply: the pawn is hard to hold, and White usually retakes with the queen, which lands on an exposed square, while Black's light-squared bishop gets out before ...e6 shuts it in. Black trades the central pawn for easy development and a solid game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto of the dark-squared bishop, which will press on the d4 pawn, and keeps the c8-bishop free to come out to f5. Black keeps the pawn tension in the centre and develops flexibly, but White gets time to build a full centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 e6 5.Nbd.strategy: Adds a second guard to c4 and supports a later e4: if Black takes on c4, the knight retakes and the queen is not chased by ...b5. The cost is that the knight blocks the c1-bishop, which suits a quiet set-up with a kingside fianchetto better than a quick central break.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 e6 5.g3.strategy: The most common set-up: the king's bishop will press on d5 and the long diagonal while the queen guards c4. If Black takes on c4, the queen retakes and Black's ...b5 gains a tempo on it. White gets a slow, flexible game with steady pressure on the light squares.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 e6 5.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 shuts it in, and presses on the knight that guards d5 and e4. The queen still guards c4, so ...dxc4 Qxc4 b5 gains Black a tempo. White plays a Queen's Gambit set-up with the e4 break in hand.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.Qc2 e6 5.Nbd.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling, waiting to see how White commits. It is a modest, solid move: Black keeps the pawn centre and all options of releasing the c8-bishop later. The price is passivity, as White gets the chance to build up slowly.

Develops the last knight, guards the knight on f6 and e5, and keeps a flexible choice for the king's bishop. Black keeps the solid pawn triangle and waits for the right moment to take on c4 or strike with ...e5, so White's e4 meets a ready defence.

Takes the pawn at once and White regains it with the knight, usually with the queen's bishop still shut in. Black gains time to play ...b5 but gives up the central pawn, and White's pieces are freer afterwards.

Chooses a fianchetto set-up: the king's bishop will sit on the long diagonal and press on d5 and the queenside. White develops quietly and keeps the tension in the centre, playing for slow pressure on the light squares rather than a quick central break.

Strikes in the centre while Black's king is still in the middle. If Black takes, the knight retakes and White has open lines and more active pieces, with the queen on a strong central square. The cost is that the centre opens before White has castled.

A solid but slow move: it opens the diagonal of the king's bishop and holds d4 firmly, but the bishop on c1 stays shut in behind its own knight and pawn. White aims for a quiet game and waits for a chance to play e4 later.

Brings out the last minor piece, backs up the knight on f6 and covers e5, so Black can castle and keep a compact, flexible structure. Black waits for the right moment to take on c4 or to hold the centre.

Brings the king to safety and connects the rooks before White's fianchetto bishop and the queen make themselves felt. Black keeps all the options for the knight on b8 and the pawn break, and the compact structure is hard to attack, at the price of giving White the first move in the middle.

Releases the tension in the centre and gives White a pawn to retake. Black gets the chance to chase the knight with ...b5 and gain queenside space, but loosens the queenside and gives up the pawn that held the centre.
